findings.title: Haste And Value
findings.claim: The focus places harm and good in the same invocation frame under a predicate of human haste. Wider passages show that good and harm do not share a humanly chosen measure: harm is not accelerated to match requests for good, desire can misread what is beneficial, and both poles can be a test. The parallel call therefore reads as hurried valuation, not as equality of outcomes.
findings.mechanism: The carriers are the focus's ordinary call for harm, its repeated call for good, and the dispositional adjective for a hasty human. They meet the supplied 10:11 contrast of human urgency with harm not advanced at the same pace, the 2:216 distinction between what is desired and what may be good or harmful, and 21:35's pairing of harm and good as a test. The 41:49 surface adds a broader call-for-good and response-under-harm pattern. The legacy_unbound walk descriptions of 17:12 and 17:18-21 supply an attributed pericope image of measured time and differentiated outcomes. Together these contacts make the identical call frame expose a skipped interval of evaluation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear why harm enters the same call-pattern as good while keeping their value and eventual outcomes distinct; haste becomes the pressure that shortens discernment.
findings.containment: The focus still states an invocation and a habitual human disposition. It does not say the caller knowingly chooses evil, that speech causes the outcome, or that desired good and harm are actually equal. 41:49 describes asking for good followed by despair when harm touches, not another call for harm. The 17:12 and 17:18-21 descriptions remain attributed because their context surfaces are not supplied, and the external connection rows provide no target morphology.

epistemic.reason: The focus surface and trusted cross-run publication ground the local call-and-haste relation. The represented walk supports are legacy_unbound, and the external connections supply exact Arabic but no target morphology; the claim therefore limits those contacts to verse-level contrasts and attributes the pericope readings.

findings.title: Calling Ahead Of Its Time
findings.claim: The focus's ordinary invocation of harm, paired with the hasty human predicate, can be read as pressing an adverse outcome toward the present. Wider passages place such urgency beside outcomes that are not brought forward at the caller's pace and beside an allotted reckoning that continues to be counted.
findings.mechanism: The carriers are the focus's call, its harm-content phrase, and its dispositional haste. They contact 38:16's supplied demand to hasten an allotted outcome before reckoning, 10:11's contrast between human haste for good and the non-accelerated harmful result, and 19:84's instruction not to hasten while counting continues. This relation changes the focus's contradiction into a prospective pressure on when an outcome arrives, while the wider count resists the caller's timetable.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the hasty invocation as an attempt to set the timing of what is coming, not only as a confused choice of what to want.
findings.containment: The focus does not name a particular punishment or promise that speech causes an event. The connection targets supply exact Arabic but no target morphology; the future-facing causal edge remains a qualified reading attributed to the legacy_unbound walk.

epistemic.reason: The candidate's own reading is legacy_unbound and identifies its causal step as an inference. The exact connection Arabic and notes independently supply temporal contrasts, but target morphology is absent and the focus does not name a specific future event.
